name: Cold water / ice to close pores

lead: Many skin-care routines end with a cold splash or a rub of ice, on the belief that cold closes pores that warmth opened, so skin looks tighter and pores look smaller.

Practitioners describe cold as tightening the skin. Dermatology references describe pores as the openings of hair follicles where sebum and keratin can form a plug, and they do not describe pores opening and closing. No published trial testing cold water or ice on pore size was identified.

paras: People finish cleansing with a splash of cold water, or wrap ice in a cloth and glide it over the face for a short time. It is also used to reduce morning puffiness and as a post-steam step.
Brief cold exposure is generally low risk. Prolonged direct ice contact on skin can irritate it, per general dermatology cautions.

chain: Cold splash or ice on face
angle.text: Splashing the face with cold water or rubbing ice on it is a long-circulating routine step meant to close pores and leave skin looking tighter. The idea comes from tradition, and no trials were found testing it.

lead: Finishing a wash with a splash of cold water, or rubbing an ice cube over the face, is a common step in skin-care routines aimed at making pores look smaller and skin look tighter and smoother. Practitioners describe warm water or steam as opening pores for cleansing and cold as closing them afterward, so the cold step is placed last.

Pores are the visible openings of hair follicles, where sebum from the sebaceous gland reaches the skin surface and where sebum and keratin can form a plug called a comedo [1][2]. Oily skin is associated with larger, more visible pores and with clogged pores and blackheads [3]. People who use cold water or ice say the cooled, slightly firmer skin and reduced shine make pores look finer for a while.

Skin-care references describe cleansing, oil control and toners as the usual tools for the look of pores, and they do not describe a mechanism by which pores open and close with temperature [3][4]. No published trial has tested cold water or ice on pore size.

paras: The practice takes two common forms: a final rinse with cold water, and rubbing an ice cube (sometimes wrapped in cloth) over the face. It is typically placed after warm washing or steaming, which proponents say loosen oil and debris, and before moisturizer or sunscreen.
Some users also use cold water after other facial routines, for example after extractions or facial massage, to calm the skin.

Proponents say pores open with warmth and close with cold, that ice tightens the skin, and that a cold rinse reduces shine on oily skin. Members of looksmax.org discussing cold-water washing have repeated the idea that it helps close pores and limit grease [5].

Skin-care references describe pores as follicle openings and note the role of sebum production in how visible they are; they do not describe muscles or other structures that open and close pores [1][2][3]. A different line of discussion on looksmax.org proposes using cold water on the eye area and hot water on the lower face for fat distribution reasons, which is a separate and unstudied theory [6].

Sebaceous glands release sebum onto the hair shaft and skin surface, and sebum with keratin can plug the follicle opening [1][2]. Blackheads are open comedones whose dark color comes from oxidation [1]. Oily skin is linked to larger-looking pores [3].
Toners and astringents are described as products meant to degrease, unclog pores and temporarily tighten the skin, and lukewarm water is the temperature usually mentioned for washing dry skin [4].
A brief cold rinse is a mild exposure. Dermatology cautions generally mention that prolonged direct ice contact can irritate or injure skin.
No studies found. Published research on cold water exposure concerns whole-body immersion in recovery and wellbeing contexts rather than facial pore appearance [7].

lore.intro: Cold water for pores comes up in looksmax.org skin-care threads as a simple habit, and in a separate thread as part of a hot-and-cold facial theory.
